div.p: Detecting brain tumors early on is critical for effective treatment and life-saving efforts. The analysis of the brain with MRI scans is fundamental to the diagnosis because it contains detailed structural views of the brain, which is vital in identifying any of its abnormalities. The other option of performing an invasive biopsy is very painful and uncomfortable, which is not the case with MRI as it is free from surgically invasive margins and pieces of equipment. This helps patients to feel more at ease and hasten the diagnostic procedure, allowing physicians to formulate and practice action plans quicker. It is very difficult to locate a human brain tumor by manual because MRI scans produce large numbers of three-dimensional images. Complete applicability of pre-written computerized diagnostics, affords high possibilities in providing areas of interest earlier through the application of machine learning techniques and algorithms. The proposed work in the present study was to develop a deep learning model which will classify brain tumor grade images (BTGC), and hence enhance accuracy in diagnosing patients with different grades of brain tumors using MRI. A MobileNetV2 model, was used to extract the features from the images. This model increases the efficiency and generalizability of the model further. In this study, six standard Kaggle brain tumor MRI datasets were used to train and validate the developed and tested model of a brain tumor detection and classification algorithm into several types. This work consists of two key components: (i) brain tumor detection and (ii) classification of the tumor. The tumor classifications are conducted in both three classes (Meningioma, Pituitary, and glioma) and two classes (malignant, benign). The model has been reported to detect brain tumors with 99.85% accuracy, to distinguish benign and malignant tumors with 99.87% accuracy, and to type meningioma, pituitary, and glioma tumors with 99.38% accuracy. The results of this study indicate that the described technique is useful in the detection and classification of brain tumors.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: e central nervous representation is typically assessed as the brain because it governs the activities of the body organs. It integrates the stimuli from the environment in form of sensory information as well as sends out messages to the different organs in the body. It is characterized by tumor formation as a result of abnormal cell division or cellular mutation. Such tumors can lead to the symptoms such as nausea, memory impairment, changes in personality, poor vision and tiredness among other features within the suppressed normal functioning of the brain [1]. Radiologists take advantage of CT and MRI as image optimizing machine for inspecting the region of the brain that has been suspected to be a tumor and proceeds to classify tumor. MRI is the most useful imaging technique to evaluate brain tumors since it is noninvasive and no instrument is used on the sensitive brain tissues. MRI is trustworthy as the results reveal every detail regarding the anatomy of the brain [2]. e use of these devices that take images at high resolution ensures that the patients are easily diagnosed properly and treatment procedures are well planned. Radiologists evaluate brain MRI scans in order to determine the presence of any tumors or a normal brain. ey divide the images into groups so as to evaluate the different types of brain tumor and the therapeutic responses they elicit. In some cases, radiologists are not only trained to read brain MRI scans but actively and manually diagnose brain tumors based on small changes within images that can be missed but are suggestive of the tumor [3].

Brain tumor detection and classification rests upon the tomographic images of the tumor, which becomes a difficult routine healthy form or a healthy cavity, then other types. Patients' adverse outcomes may be due to the unavailability of efficient and appropriate staff [4]. To these factors, there is an extra pressure on radiologists to help them develop more accurate and faster techniques for tumor detection and classification. Even in the absence of working diagnostic imaging equipment, attempting to perform tumor diagnosis and classification inherently suffers from a lack of adequate and time-tested methods. e utilization of a computerized aid for diagnosis (CAD) should facilitate the radiologists in accurately detecting and classifying the brain tumors as it eases the discomforts experienced due to the hand methods employed. Gliomas, pituitary adenomas, and meningiomas are examples of benign and malignant brain tumors [6]. Distinct tumor type and level is critical in the situation of brain tumors. Benign tumors increase slowly without invading other organs while the cancerous ones are aggressive and invade other body areas within the shortest time possible and if untreated a possibility of metastasis is very high. Two kinds of malignant tumors are most feared than the others where one is primary malignant tumors which originate in the central nervous system (CNS) and secondary malignant ones which metastasize into the CNS from other sites [7].

Primary malignancies are those that develop within the brain. Primary brain tumors include meningioma, pituitary adenoma, and glioma types. Meningiomas are usually benign tumors of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. Low-grade gliomas and pituitary tumors are either benign or cancerous depending on the conditions [8]. Efficient feature extraction techniques make it possible to retrieve the expected patterns and spatial relations in the MR images, for example, the detection of the shape and surface pattern of tumors [12]. div.head: Key novelties
div.p: e model presented for the detection and classification of brain tumors has introduced new features such as:

• Using MobileNetV2 for Feature Extraction: Mobile-NetV2, which was designed for efficiency and generalizability, is a lightweight model which can leverage templates and perform background tasks in deep learning. Even so, regarding its application in MRI images; the model is especially suited for real-time or limited-resource contexts, as its precision is not sacrificed.

• Comprehensive Brain Tumor Classification: However, the model does binary classification (malignant or benign) as well as multiclass classification (Meningioma, Pituitary, Glioma) thereby improving its diagnostic capability. is extends the usability of the system for different clinical requirements which assists in specificity in diagnosis.

• High Accuracy Across Tasks: Considering the accuracies of 99.85% for detection, 99.87% for binary classification and 99.38% for multiclass classification, it can be said that the performance is impressive and still acceptable for purposes where automatic systems are performing the task of diagnosis on brain tumors. • Application of Six Kaggle Datasets: By training and validating the model with six standard Kaggle brain tumor MRI datasets, the model becomes robust and exhibits better generalization due to its exposure to various real case instances.

• Non-Invasive, Faster Diagnosis: e model will leverage biomedical imaging and machine learning so that invasive procedures such as biopsy will not be necessary, enabling faster and non-invasive diagnostic methods to be used in the clinic for accelerated treatment decision making.

Challenges in automated methods of detection and classification of brain tumors include reliance on manual definition of tumor zone which lowers surgical consistency as well as scale in tumor diagnosis and variety of images used, among others. DL methods which absorb significant number of features extracted from medical images have the potential to reduce the inefficiency and inaccuracy of tumor classification tasks. Nevertheless, it is unrealistic to utilize such sophisticated machine learning algorithms in real practice due to high demands on memory and calculation. Often, images obtained through medical investigation are done in a limited number, or in an unbalanced way. eir performance and generalizability may be hampered, particularly for DL methods. Low performance and generalizability of advanced machine learning models may be attributed to insufficient labelled data for rare tumors or tumor-related patient populations. is is critical in neuro-oncology where treatment and outcome plans require accurate targeting of various types of brain tumors. Some of the recent efforts have been to evaluate and rank the existing algorithms using publicly available datasets including Figshare in attempts to address the question of how well existing algorithms perform complex tasks like brain tumor classification.

is research proposes a novel approach called Brain Tumor Grade Classification (BTGC) system which seeks to overcome the burden of classifying and diagnosing various grades of brain tumors owing to their differences in size, shape and position. BTGC model employs improved architecture of the MobileNet starting with 32-3 × 3 kernel convolution on the first two full convolutional layers. Further, in order to achieve complicated features, an additional processing layer of 14 is required employing Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) for their activation. Moreover, there are average pooling and dropout layers employed to boost the model's performance and tackle overfitting, thus making the network smaller and improving the generalizability of the model. e performance of the BTGC model is aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of automated systems in analyzing brain tumor by utilizing advanced design features and optimization techniques. It is a part of neuroimaging development and will help make more precise diagnoses and devise optimal treatment schemes in neurology and oncology. e article's remaining sections are shown below. "Related work" section offers a summary of the relevant literature, while "Material and methods" section explains the approach that was used. "Experimental Results and Discussion" section provides details of the tests carried out for performance evaluation. "Conclusion" section presents the concluding analysis and interpretation of the work.

div.head: Proposed Brain Tumor Grade Classification (BTGC)
div.p: In this study, the BTGC model has been developed to identify and classify glioma brain tumors using Goog-LeNet for classification and MobileNet for feature extraction. Both GoogLeNet and MobileNet are CNN architectures fully elaborated and equipped and that bring excellent results in image classification.

e aim of this study was to create a tool that would be able to detect and classify brain tumors without the need for prior segmentation, dissection, machination, and other tedious and tedious preparative measures. An overview of the model in comparison with the standard ones is presented in Table 3, which shows that the model has a configuration more than that of the standard CNNs in addition, this model has 49 learnable layers, 129 feature extraction levels and 5 classification levels. Standard CNNs consist of 48 convolutional and 1 fully connected layer. In order to decrease the computational complexity, the first layer, which is an image input layer, accepts the images of a shape 224 × 224.

ere's a 134-layer model structure, which contains 48 layers for batch normalization (no Adam here only in our proposed one), 4 for LReLU, 28 for ReLU, one for global average pooling then dropout, fully connected, softmax and classification layer.

e model includes 28 ReLU layers and 4 LReLU layers. A dropout rate of 0.4% is applied to the fully connected layer to prevent overfitting. Computational efficiency is achieved through five convolutional layers with a 2 × 2 stride, reducing spatial resolution. e design begins with a 32-kernel fully convolutional layer, followed by 15 residual bottleneck layers. Following the initial fully convolutional and residual bottleneck levels, there are fourteen additional layers using the ReLU activation function, with the final two layers employing LReLU.

e remaining bottleneck layers consist of two types of filters: one with a 1 × 1 size and another with a 3 × 3 size. ese small filters extract important features from the MRI data. Next, there is a batch normalisation layer with an epsilon of 0.001 and an activation function, with LReLU for the first residual bottleneck layer and ReLU for the other fourteen levels. ese layers begin with a first convolution (1 × 1 filter).

div.head: Ablation study
div.p: An ablation study was performed to understand the contribution of various elements of the proposed deep learning architecture for the classification of brain tumor grade images (BTGC) to the overall performance of the system.

e baseline BTGC model mainly includes a stack of forty-eight convolution layers with leaky ReLU (LReLU) and ReLU activations, an average pooling layer, a dropout layer, a fully connected layer, and softmax layer. e model was tested for efficiency on six standard Kaggle MRI datasets of the brain tumor to find the presence, type and grade of the tumor benign or malignant mesothelioma, glioma, pituitary and meningioma. e baseline model reached almost 100% level of accuracy in relation to the detection of the presence of the tumor -99.85%, the ability to classify tumors as benign and malignant -99.87% and 98.36% in categorizing glioma, pituitary and meningioma tumors. e ablation study focused on performing the following exercises to investigate the effect of different parameters constituting the deep learning model on its performance.
